seoTitle: How to Add MX Records in Hostinger to Connect Gmail
metaDescription: Learn how to add MX records in Hostinger's DNS zone to route your domain's email through Gmail, Zoho Mail, or another provider without downtime.
intro: If you registered a domain with Hostinger but want email handled by Gmail, Zoho Mail, or another provider, the fix lives in one small form buried inside the domain's DNS settings. This guide walks through that exact form — the same one used to add A records or any other DNS entry — and shows what changes once you switch the record type to MX. Getting the mail server value and priority right the first time is what saves you from bounced mail and a long wait to find out something was typed wrong.

steps.heading: Log in and select the domain you're configuring
steps.body: Sign in to Hostinger and land in hPanel, the dashboard for everything domain- and hosting-related. If you manage more than one domain, use the domain selector at the top of the sidebar to pick the correct one before touching any records — MX records are set per domain, so working in the wrong one silently does nothing for the site you actually meant to fix.

steps.heading: Open DNS / Nameservers for that domain
steps.body: With the right domain selected, click DNS / Nameservers in the left sidebar. This is the single section that controls how the domain resolves and routes traffic, covering everything from the A records that point to a web server to the MX records that route mail — there's no separate "email settings" area to hunt for.

image.caption: hPanel's sidebar with a domain selected and DNS / Nameservers highlighted as the active section.

steps.heading: Find the Manage DNS records form
steps.body: Scroll to "Manage DNS records," a short form for adding any entry: a Type dropdown, a Name field, a value field, and a TTL. By default the Type is set to A, with Name defaulting to @ (meaning the root domain) and a "Points to" field for an IP address — this is the same form you'd use to point the domain at a web server, just with a different record type selected.

image.caption: The Manage DNS records form with Type set to A, Name set to @, and a Points to field for an IP address.

steps.heading: Switch the record type to MX
steps.body: Open the Type dropdown and choose MX. The form reshapes itself the moment you do — the "Points to" field becomes "Mail server," and a new Priority field appears between it and TTL, since mail servers (unlike A records) can be ranked so a domain can list a backup. This is where you type in the mail server value your provider gives you, such as the address Gmail or Zoho Mail supplies for custom domain routing.

image.caption: The same DNS form after switching Type to MX, now showing a Mail server field and a Priority field set to 10.

steps.heading: Fill in the mail server, priority, and TTL
steps.body: Name stays as @ for the root domain in most setups. Mail server is the value from your provider — for Gmail-hosted domains this is typically their published mail exchange address, and Zoho Mail supplies its own equivalent. Priority defaults to 10, and lower numbers mean higher priority, which matters if you ever list more than one mail server. TTL controls how long the record is cached before DNS servers re-check it; the default of 14400 seconds is fine for most setups, and lowering it only helps if you're actively troubleshooting and want changes to take effect faster.

steps.heading: Save the record
steps.body: Click Add Record once every field is filled in correctly. Hostinger adds it to the domain's DNS zone immediately on their end, but that's only the first half of the process — the record still has to spread across the wider DNS system before mail actually starts routing through it.

steps.heading: Wait for propagation, then test
steps.body: DNS changes typically take anywhere from a few minutes to several hours to fully propagate, depending on caching along the way. Once enough time has passed, send a test email to an address on the domain or use a DNS lookup tool to confirm the MX record is visible and pointing where you expect. If mail still isn't arriving after propagation should be complete, recheck the mail server value and priority for typos before assuming something else is broken.

faq.question: How long does it take for MX records to work after adding them in Hostinger?
faq.answer: Propagation usually takes anywhere from a few minutes up to several hours, depending on your previous DNS settings and TTL value.

faq.question: Can I use Gmail and Zoho Mail on the same Hostinger domain?
faq.answer: You can only route mail through one email provider at a time per domain, since MX records point to a single mail server setup; switching providers means replacing the old MX records.

faq.question: What priority number should I use for MX records?
faq.answer: Lower numbers indicate higher priority; Hostinger's form defaults to 10, but most providers tell you the exact priority to enter for each mail server they list.

faq.question: Why isn't my email working after adding MX records?
faq.answer: This is usually a propagation delay or a typo in the mail server value or priority, so double-check the values against your provider's instructions and wait before testing again.

faq.question: Do I need to change the Name field when adding an MX record?
faq.answer: For most domains you leave Name as @, which points the record at the root domain rather than a subdomain, unless your provider specifically instructs otherwise.
